_comment: The kingdoms themselves. Borders are SCHEMATIC — simplified from the archaeological picture (Finkelstein & Silberman; Lipschits; the biblical description for the biblical layer). They communicate extent and change, not survey-grade boundaries. mode 'biblical' = the literary picture, 'archaeological' = the material record, 'both' = shared. start/end are BCE years.

popup.bible: From Dan to Beersheba — a golden empire. David conquers from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt; Solomon's kingdom 'held dominion over all the region west of the Euphrates' (1 Kgs 4:21-24).
popup.archaeology: The empire the ground does not know. No trace of a 10th-century state from Dan to Beersheba: no inscriptions, no monumental cities, no evidence of conquest. Jerusalem itself was a small highland town.

popup.bible: The Bible's empire was here — in this one hill town.
popup.archaeology: What archaeology actually finds in the 10th century: a chiefdom centered on Jerusalem, a town of a few thousand people with no monumental architecture. The surrounding region stayed Canaanite and independent.

popup.bible: The breakaway north under Jeroboam I: Shechem and then Tirzah as capitals, golden calves at Dan and Bethel (1 Kgs 12).
popup.archaeology: The northern highlands show dense settlement and early state formation — the north was always the demographic heavyweight.

popup.bible: The 'evil' kings of the Bible — Omri, Ahab, Jehu — who built Samaria, married Phoenicia, and fought Assyria at Qarqar with 2,000 chariots.
popup.archaeology: A real state at its height: the Omride dynasty's monuments (Samaria, Jezreel, Megiddo's 9th-century gates), control of the Jezreel Valley and the coastal trade, and a province in Transjordan. Assyria calls it Bit-Humri — the House of Omri.
popup.source: Kurkh Monolith; Black Obelisk; Finkelstein & Silberman

popup.bible: After Tiglath-Pileser III strips away Galilee and Gilead, all that is left of Israel is 'the city of Samaria' and its hills (2 Kgs 17:5-6).
popup.archaeology: The Assyrian provincial reorganization leaves a rump around Samaria until Sargon II finishes the job in 722 — deporting 27,290 people, by his own count.

popup.bible: The little south that outlasted the mighty north: the House of David ruling Jerusalem, the temple, and the Shephelah's fortress cities.
popup.archaeology: A modest but real kingdom: fortified cities (Lachish, Beersheba, Arad), the royal administration, and — after 722 — a demographic boom as northern refugees flood south. Then Sennacherib strips the Shephelah in 701.

popup.bible: Jerusalem survives the siege of 701 — 'the angel of the Lord struck down 185,000 Assyrians' (2 Kgs 19:35). The city grows, and the temple's treasury pays the tribute.
popup.archaeology: Sennacherib's prism tells the other side: he took 46 walled cities and shut Hezekiah 'like a bird in a cage.' Judah shrinks to the hill country around Jerusalem — which then triples in size as refugees flood in. This is the Judah that Josiah reforms.

popup.bible: The northern kingdom gone — deported, scattered, 'the ten lost tribes.' The farmers left behind become, in time, the Samaritans (2 Kgs 17:24-41).
popup.archaeology: Sargon II's inscription: 'I conquered Samaria and carried away 27,290 people.' Samaria becomes an Assyrian provincial capital, and the northern kingdom never returns.
